name: Azure Managed Identity Token Theft (VM IMDS)
description: From code execution on an Azure VM (or App Service/Function) that has a managed identity, request an access token from the Instance Metadata Service (IMDS), then authenticate as that identity. Managed identities frequently hold RBAC roles, so this is a common privilege-escalation / lateral-movement pivot.
source: MCRTA (CyberWarFare Labs) - Multi-Cloud Red Team Analyst: Azure

examples.label: Request an ARM token for the VM's managed identity
Use the stolen token in Az PowerShell
Enumerate what the managed identity can do
Token for Microsoft Graph instead of ARM

notes: IMDS (169.254.169.254) is reachable only from ON the instance and requires the 'Metadata:true' header (blocks naive SSRF that can't set headers - but header-controlling SSRF CAN reach it). Change &resource= to target ARM (management.azure.com) or Graph (graph.microsoft.com) - request a token per resource. System-assigned vs user-assigned identity: for user-assigned add &client_id=<id> or &mi_res_id=<resource_id>. After Connect-AzAccount with the token, you act as the managed identity at its RBAC scope - check Get-AzRoleAssignment for Contributor/Owner to escalate. Classic chain: web SSRF on an Azure VM -> IMDS token -> ARM access.

references.title: Microsoft Learn - Azure Instance Metadata Service

recommended.note: Enumerate ARM with the stolen identity
SSRF that can set headers can reach IMDS remotely

defense.why_it_works: A VM with an attached managed identity can request OAuth tokens for that identity from the local IMDS endpoint without any secret. Any code (or header-controlling SSRF) running on the instance can obtain a token and then act as the managed identity, inheriting whatever RBAC roles it holds - often far more than the compromised app needs.
defense.prerequisites: Code execution on (or header-controlling SSRF against) an Azure VM/App Service/Function that has a system- or user-assigned managed identity with RBAC assignments.
defense.impact: T1552.005 Unsecured Credentials: Cloud Instance Metadata API + T1078.004 Valid Accounts: Cloud Accounts. The attacker acts as the managed identity across ARM/Graph - privilege escalation and lateral movement into the subscription.
defense.detection: Azure Activity Log: managed-identity principal performing actions from an unexpected context/time; token requests followed by anomalous ARM/Graph calls; Defender for Cloud IMDS/credential-theft alerts. SSRF patterns hitting 169.254.169.254 in web logs.
defense.artifacts: Activity Log entries by the managed identity's principalId; token issuance to the MI; web logs with requests to 169.254.169.254.
defense.splunk_spl:
index=azure sourcetype="azure:audit" operationName="Acquire access token" OR operationName="Add managed identity credential"
| table _time, identity.claims.name, targetResources{}.displayName, result

index=azure sourcetype="azure:signin" authenticationDetails{}.authenticationMethod="ManagedIdentity"
| stats count by identity, resourceDisplayName, ipAddress
defense.elastic_kql:
event.dataset:azure.auditlogs AND event.action:(*managed*identity* OR *access*token*)

event.dataset:azure.signinlogs AND azure.signinlogs.properties.authentication_details.method:ManagedIdentity
defense.sentinel_kql:
AzureActivity
| where Caller has "managedidentity" or CallerIpAddress != ""
| project TimeGenerated, OperationNameValue, Caller, CallerIpAddress
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
// IMDS token request (169.254.169.254) followed by anomalous ARM/Graph calls by the MI principal
defense.prevention: Least-privilege the managed identity (scope to exactly what the app needs). Use IMDSv-style protections / restrict metadata access (host firewall/eBPF) for workloads that don't need it. Fix SSRF (allowlist egress, block link-local 169.254.0.0/16). Monitor MI usage anomalies.
defense.evasion: Use the token quickly and from expected operations; request only the resource you need; blend with the app's normal ARM/Graph calls.
defense.misconfiguration: Over-privileged managed identity (e.g., Contributor at subscription scope) on an internet-facing VM/app; SSRF that can set request headers.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# MI with Contributor at subscription, app has SSRF -> attacker sets Metadata header via SSRF:
# GET http://169.254.169.254/metadata/identity/oauth2/token?...&resource=https://management.azure.com/ (Metadata:true)
defense.secure_config:
# Scope the managed identity to least privilege (specific resource group / resource).
# Block workload egress to 169.254.169.254 where the app does not need IMDS.
# Remediate SSRF (egress allowlist, block link-local); alert on MI anomalies in Activity Log.

validation.success_criteria: At least one behavioral detection fires within 60 seconds of attack execution
response_steps: Correlate alert with source host, user account, and timestamp
Review Azure Activity Log, Windows Security Event Log for surrounding context (5 min before/after)
Check for credential dumping artifacts (LSASS access, SAM hive reads, Kerberos anomalies)
Verify whether the activity matches known administrative baselines or change windows
If confirmed malicious, isolate the host and escalate to incident response

explain:
Steals an Azure VM's managed-identity token from the Instance Metadata Service:
  curl -H "Metadata:true"   the required IMDS header
  "http://169.254.169.254/metadata/identity/oauth2/token?api-version=2018-02-01&resource=https://management.azure.com/"   request an ARM access token for the VM's managed identity
From code execution on the VM, this returns a bearer token; use it against the Azure APIs as that identity, which frequently holds RBAC roles.
